faqs.q: Are armadillos really established around Florence?

We trap the animals working your property and backfill and screen the burrow openings, because an open burrow in this soil is quickly claimed by the next armadillo — or by a skunk or opossum.

faqs.q: Something is digging up my Florence lawn at night and it smells like skunk. What is going on?
faqs.a: That combination is a striped skunk hunting grubs — the small cone-shaped holes across a lawn are its signature — and a den under a porch, deck, or crawlspace edge is usually nearby. Skunks are South Carolina's number-two rabies carrier in Department of Public Health testing, and routine relocation is against state law, so our crew traps calmly at the den with covered traps, handles the animal under SCDNR depredation rules, and screens the den opening so the next skunk finds it closed.

faqs.q: We found an opossum in our Timmonsville crawlspace. What happens next?
faqs.a: In Timmonsville, opossums move into crawlspaces through broken vents and loose doors, then rotate dens every few days, which is why sightings come and go. We trap at the access point, remove the animal under SCDNR depredation rules, and seal the full foundation line. Securing pet food and trash at night removes the other half of the attraction.

faqs.q: Pigeons and starlings are nesting in my Timmonsville vents. Can they be removed?
faqs.a: Pigeons, European starlings, and house sparrows are the birds we can work on in Timmonsville — vents screened, nests cleared, and spikes or netting fitted so the birds move on. Native birds are different: woodpeckers, chimney swifts, and nesting songbirds are protected under the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, so those jobs are deterrence and timing, waiting out the nest and sealing after the young fledge. Around tobacco-town streets and farm roads west of Florence, vent and soffit nests are the calls we see most.

faqs.q: How do you price the work on a Timmonsville home?

Attic contamination, the number of openings to seal in steel, crawlspace repairs, and whether the job needs return visits for trapping all shape the work. We itemize what we find, explain which items stop the problem for good and which are optional, and let you decide with the full list in hand.

Timmonsville.wildlife_intro:
Ask around Timmonsville and the wildlife stories usually trace back to the tobacco-town streets and farm roads west of Florence. Homeowners here phone us first about armadillos in sandy field-edge yards, then about bats in tobacco-barn and gable roosts.

Housing here runs from historic in-town streets to farm roads, and most of it predates modern sealed construction — open vents and pier foundations are the norm. Blackwater rivers and swamp drains thread this farm country, and wildlife follows them: raccoons, opossums, and armadillos work the wet edges, then den in the nearest barn, porch, or crawlspace.

Before we leave a Timmonsville home, the roofline, foundation line, and any outbuilding we worked on get rechecked opening by opening — that recheck is what keeps one call from becoming three.

faqs.q: Why do squirrels keep getting into Johnsonville attics?

faqs.q: How does bat removal work in Pamplico?
faqs.a: In Pamplico, bat work means exclusion only: one-way devices on the main entries, every other opening sealed, and the colony leaves on its own at dusk. South Carolina does not require a permit for bat removal, and we time full exclusions to SCDNR's guidance windows — early spring or August through October — to avoid trapping flightless young during the summer maternity season. Guano cleanup follows once the attic is empty.

faqs.q: Something is rooting up my Pamplico lawn in strips. Is that an armadillo?
faqs.a: Torn-up strips of turf and a burrow mouth about the width of a dinner plate point to a nine-banded armadillo, a species now established across all of South Carolina. In Pamplico we trap at the active burrow, then collapse, backfill, and screen the opening so the next animal cannot reopen it. Simply filling a burrow without screening rarely holds in this soil for more than a few weeks.

faqs.q: What does a wildlife removal job in Pamplico actually involve?
faqs.a: It starts with the inspection, and the scope grows or shrinks with what that inspection finds around Great Pee Dee River-side farms south of Florence: how many entry points the animal has opened, whether young are present, and how much exclusion the roofline and crawlspace need. A single squirrel entry sealed in a day is a small job; a raccoon family with latrine cleanup and a full roofline seal is a larger one. We walk you through each item we find before the work is set, so the scope you approve is the scope we do.

Pamplico.wildlife_intro:
Our Pamplico calls cluster near the Great Pee Dee River-side farms south of Florence. The calls we run most are opossums and raccoons around grain and feed storage and armadillos rooting lawns.

Early-1900s farm-town housing, tobacco-era homes, and postwar ranches sit on crawlspaces above soil that stays damp much of the year. Flat, wet ground after summer storms pushes snakes and burrowing animals onto higher, drier lots — frequently the lots with houses on them — which is when many of our calls here start.

We finish Pamplico jobs by closing the route, not just removing the animal — vents screened, soffits rebuilt, crawlspace doors latched and framed — because the woods behind these streets will test every weak point again.

faqs.q: I saw a snake near my Coward home. Should I be worried?
faqs.a: Most snakes our crew is called about here are harmless rat snakes, black racers, and garter snakes following rodents and frogs. The ones that change the call are the copperhead, which is statewide, and — only in the wet coastal and swamp country — the cottonmouth. We identify first, from a safe distance: keep kids and pets inside, do not try to move or kill it, and tell us where it went. The southern hognose snake of the Sandhills is State Threatened and is never handled as a removal job, and venomous snakes are safety-and-referral work, not a guaranteed capture.
